question: to the Commission Pina Picierno (S&D) Subject:
Exclusion of Keshet Italia from Rome Pride 2026 and anti-Semitism in civil rights movements

Keshet Italia has been excluded from Rome Pride 2026: having initially been prevented from joining the organising committee responsible for drafting the event’s political manifesto, the Jewish LGBTQIA+ group was then barred from entering a float in the parade. Rome Pride organisers say that they made this decision after Keshet refused to sign the event manifesto condemning ‘the Israeli State’s ongoing genocide in Gaza’1 – a form of ‘political vetting’ that raises strong suspicions of double standards. Keshet refused the organisers’ invitation to join the parade on foot on security grounds, seeing as its members were labelled as ‘assassins’2 and ‘terrorists’3 and assaulted during last year’s march after they had unfurled rainbow Star of David flags – an incident which Rome Pride did not condemn. While the Jewish organisation has criticised what it calls ‘an anti-Semitic act masquerading as a political stance’4, Rome Pride’s bias has not prevented the Municipality of Rome from patronising this year’s event. In the light of the above, we ask the Commission: 1.

Does it hold that excluding a Jewish organisation from a public event is a form of discrimination prohibited by Article 21 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU, and will it consider launching a monitoring procedure against Italy under Article 2 TEU?

Will it take steps to ensure that events sponsored or funded by public bodies in the Member States cannot exclude participants on the basis of their ethnic or religious identity, a violation of Directive 2000/43/EC on racial equality?

answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (31.7.2026) The Commission is fully committed to promote and build a Union of Equality and has adopted the LGBTIQ+1 Equality Strategy 2026-20302 and the Strategy on combating antisemitism and fostering Jewish life 2021-20303. Freedom of expression, freedom of assembly and association and the right to nondiscrimination are fundamental rights enshrined in the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union4. They also constitute the essential foundations of European democracy and are foundational values enshrined in the Treaties5. The definition and application of rules governing the holding of demonstrations is a matter that pertains to the Member States6. The Charter applies to Member States when they are implementing EU law, in line with its Article 51(1). Outside the implementation of EU law, it is for Member States, including their judicial authorities, to ensure that fundamental rights are effectively respected and protected, in accordance with their national legislation and international human rights obligations. With regard to Council Directive 2000/43/EC7, it offers protection against discrimination on the grounds of racial or ethnic origin in certain well-defined fields, namely employment and vocational training, social protection, social advantages, education and access to and supply of goods and services, including housing. The Directive does not cover the organisation of public events which remains a national competence.
